title: Dimensional crossover and local strain induced deflection of the spin spiral state in multiferroic NiI2
authors: Tianxing Jiang, Lianchuang Li, Haiyan Zhu, Hongyu Wang, Junchao Tian, Wenzhao Wang, Weiyi Pan, Haitao Wang, Changlin Zheng, Hongjun Xiang, Changsong Xu, Donglai Feng, Tong Zhang
abstract: Low-dimensional multiferroics hold great promise for integrated magnetoelectric devices. Spin spiral state has recently been shown to induce ferroelectricity in single-layer van der Waals (vdW) material NiI2. However, how this state evolves and can be tuned towards the two-dimensional limit remain unclear. Here, we combine spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy, layer-by-layer film growth, and multi-scale theoretical modeling to investigate the spin spirals in NiI2 thin films. As the film thickness increases from 1 to 7 monolayers, we observed a continuous increase of spin-spiral wavelength and a rotation of wavevector from near [110] to [1-10] direction, which evidences a dimensional crossover primarily driven by enhanced interlayer exchange energy. Moreover, we find that the film wrinkles can cause deflection of the spin spiral wavevector, which is caused by local curvature induced modification of exchange interactions. Our findings establish thickness and local strain as two tuning methods for engineering non-collinear helical magnetism and accompanied electric polarization in vdW multiferroics.
summary: This work systematically explores how the magnetic spin spiral state in layered multiferroic NiI2 responds to changes in film thickness and mechanical strain. By combining advanced STM measurements with detailed theoretical modeling, the authors establish that both dimensionality crossover and local curvature are powerful methods for engineering non-collinear magnetism and associated ferroelectricity in these 2D materials.
main_problem: The study investigates how the spin spiral state, which induces ferroelectricity, evolves as a function of film thickness and local strain in few-layer multiferroic NiI2.
main_result: Thickness increases cause a dimensional crossover characterized by an increasing spin-spiral wavelength and wavevector rotation. Furthermore, local film wrinkles induce measurable deflection of the spin spiral wavevector due to modified exchange interactions.
method: The research combines experimental techniques like Spin-Polarized STM with advanced theoretical modeling using DFT+U calculations and spin-lattice dynamics simulations (LAMMPS/SpinGNN++).
model_or_system: The physical system is few-layer van der Waals multiferroic NiI2, modeled by incorporating complex magnetic interactions including Heisenberg, Kitaev, and biquadratic terms. The Hamiltonian describes the coupled spin-lattice dynamics across different stacking orders (AA, AB, AC).
key_observables: Spin-spiral wavelength ($\lambda$), wavevector ($\mathbf{q}$) rotation/deflection, interlayer exchange coupling strength ($J_{nn}^\perp$), and associated electric polarization.
important_parameters: Film thickness (1 to 7 ML), local strain/curvature, Hubbard correction parameter U=4.0 eV, and various magnetic exchange parameters ($J_1, K$, etc.).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mapping interlayer interactions onto effective intralayer couplings and assuming that structural changes dictate the modification of magnetic exchange interactions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate lattice structures, STM images showing spin spirals, and energy diagrams comparing different stacking orders (AA, AB, AC) and the effect of curvature-induced strain on magnetism.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the basic thickness dependence using SP-STM data, then developing a comprehensive theoretical model incorporating multiple interactions, and finally demonstrating how local mechanical strain (wrinkles/curvature) acts as an additional tuning knob for the magnetic state.
why_interesting: While focused on magnetism, the coupling between structural deformation (strain/curvature) and electronic/magnetic ordering is central to modern condensed matter physics, relevant for understanding emergent phenomena in low-dimensional quantum materials.
